text_blocks.snippet: The debt ceiling was reinstated on January 2, 2025, following its suspension through January 1, 2025. The ceiling was initially set at $36.1 trillion, which was the amount of debt outstanding on that date. The Treasury Department then began using "extraordinary measures" to manage the government's finances and avoid a default. These measures are expected to be exhausted sometime between June and August, with an "X-date" likely in August.

list.title: Suspension:
list.snippet: The debt ceiling was suspended as part of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, which was signed into law in July 2025.

list.title: Reinstatement:
list.snippet: The suspension ended on January 1, 2025, and the debt ceiling was reinstated on January 2, 2025, at the existing debt level of $36.1 trillion.

list.title: Extraordinary Measures:
list.snippet: The Treasury Department began using accounting techniques to manage the government's cash flow and avoid defaulting on its obligations, as the debt had reached the limit.

list.title: "X-Date":
list.snippet: The "X-date" refers to the point when the Treasury will no longer be able to meet all of its financial obligations due to the debt ceiling.

list.title: Potential Default:
list.snippet: If Congress does not raise or suspend the debt ceiling before the extraordinary measures are exhausted, the U.S. could default on its debt.

list.title: July 2025 Legislation:
list.snippet: In July 2025, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which raised the debt ceiling by $5 trillion to $41.1 trillion, likely delaying another debt ceiling showdown for a year or two.
